claim: Embryos have been documented refining arm-to-mouth reaching movements in utero.
source: Learning to move our limbs precisely and accurately begins in utero, where embryos have been documented refining arm-to-mouth reaching movements (Zoia et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to Zoia et al., 2007

claim: The trajectory of optimizing reaching across infancy is highly protracted.
source: The trajectory of optimizing reaching across infancy (Berthier and Keen, 2006; Leed et al., 2019) and childhood (Contreras-Vidal, 2006; Schneiberg et al., 2002; Simon-Martinez et al., 2018; Sveistrup et al., 2008) is highly protracted, roughly plateauing at around 10–12 years of age.
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to developmental studies

claim: Reaching optimization roughly plateaus at around 10-12 years of age.
source: The trajectory of optimizing reaching across infancy (Berthier and Keen, 2006; Leed et al., 2019) and childhood (Contreras-Vidal, 2006; Schneiberg et al., 2002; Simon-Martinez et al., 2018; Sveistrup et al., 2008) is highly protracted, roughly plateauing at around 10–12 years of age.
evidence: Supported by citations to developmental studies

claim: The brain is more plastic during earlier stages of development.
source: It is often thought that the brain is more plastic during earlier stages of development (Knudsen, 2004).
evidence: Supported by citation to Knudsen, 2004

claim: It becomes more difficult to acquire radically new motor skills in adulthood.
source: Therefore, it becomes more difficult to acquire radically new motor skills in adulthood, which is probably why most virtuoso musicians and athletes started practicing their trade in their childhood (Penhune, 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Penhune, 2011

claim: Most virtuoso musicians and athletes started practicing their trade in childhood.
source: Therefore, it becomes more difficult to acquire radically new motor skills in adulthood, which is probably why most virtuoso musicians and athletes started practicing their trade in their childhood (Penhune, 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Penhune, 2011

claim: In the study sample, individuals with congenital limb difference started using artificial arms as early as 3 months with an average of approximately 2.5 years.
source: As mentioned above, individuals with a congenital limb difference start using artificial arms at a very young age (in our sample as early as 3 months with an average of ~2.5 years), even before early training for musical and athletic skills.
evidence: Based on data collected from the study participants

claim: In the study sample, individuals with acquired limb difference began using artificial arms at a mean age of 32 years.
source: It therefore stands to reason that in comparison to the acquired group, who only begin to learn to use their artificial arm as adults (in our sample at a mean age of 32), the congenital group should have had more time and practice in early childhood to perfect their artificial arm motor skill.
evidence: Based on data collected from the study participants

claim: Individuals with an acquired limb difference often experience a 'phantom hand'.
source: Moreover, individuals with an acquired limb difference often experience a 'phantom hand' (Stankevicius et al., 2021), rooted in a maintained representation of their missing arm (Bruurmijn et al., 2017; Kikkert et al., 2016; Wesselink et al., 2019) which might in theory interfere with the acquisition of a representation of an arm substitute (the artificial arm).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies

claim: Phantom hand experience is rooted in a maintained representation of the missing arm.
source: Moreover, individuals with an acquired limb difference often experience a 'phantom hand' (Stankevicius et al., 2021), rooted in a maintained representation of their missing arm (Bruurmijn et al., 2017; Kikkert et al., 2016; Wesselink et al., 2019) which might in theory interfere with the acquisition of a representation of an arm substitute (the artificial arm).
evidence: Supported by citations to Bruurmijn et al., 2017; Kikkert et al., 2016; Wesselink et al., 2019

claim: Individuals with a congenital limb difference tend to make better use of their artificial arm in daily life compared to individuals with an acquired limb difference.
source: Perhaps most importantly, relative to individuals with an acquired limb difference, individuals with a congenital limb difference tend to make better use of their artificial arm in daily life (Biddiss and Chau, 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to Biddiss and Chau, 2007

claim: Children born with high-density cataracts who received corrective surgery later in life retain some rudimentary forms of visual perception.
source: For example, in the visual domain, children born with high-density cataracts who received corrective surgery later in life have been shown to retain some rudimentary forms of visual perception (Gandhi et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Gandhi et al., 2017

claim: The neural topographical organization of sensory input across the cortex is in part determined by genetics.
source: The neural topographical organization of sensory input across the cortex has been shown to be in part determined by genetics (Miyashita-Lin et al., 1999; Rubenstein et al., 1999).
evidence: Supported by citations to Miyashita-Lin et al., 1999; Rubenstein et al., 1999

claim: Early deprivation has been shown to have a permanent effect on development for both the motor system and the visual system.
source: However, for both the motor system and the visual system (an integral input to the sensorimotor loop), early deprivation has been shown to have a permanent effect on development (de Heering et al., 2016; Walton et al., 1992).
evidence: Supported by citations to de Heering et al., 2016; Walton et al., 1992

claim: The congenital group started training to use an artificial arm earlier in life than the acquired group.
source: we found that although the congenital group started using an artificial arm as toddlers, they produced increased error noise and directional errors when reaching to visual targets, relative to the acquired group who performed similarly to controls.
evidence: Based on study design and participant demographics

claim: The congenital group sustained more elapsed years of artificial arm use than the acquired group.
source: we found that although they had started training to use an artificial arm earlier in life and sustained more elapsed years of artificial arm use, individuals with a congenital limb difference were unable to refine their reaching control to normal levels.
evidence: Based on study participant demographics

claim: The congenital group produced increased error noise when reaching to visual targets relative to the acquired group.
source: we found that although the congenital group started using an artificial arm as toddlers, they produced increased error noise and directional errors when reaching to visual targets, relative to the acquired group who performed similarly to controls.
evidence: Based on experimental data from the main reaching task

claim: The congenital group produced increased directional errors when reaching to visual targets relative to the acquired group.
source: we found that although the congenital group started using an artificial arm as toddlers, they produced increased error noise and directional errors when reaching to visual targets, relative to the acquired group who performed similarly to controls.
evidence: Based on experimental data from the main reaching task

claim: The acquired group performed similarly to controls in the reaching task.
source: we found that although the congenital group started using an artificial arm as toddlers, they produced increased error noise and directional errors when reaching to visual targets, relative to the acquired group who performed similarly to controls.
evidence: Based on experimental data from the main reaching task

claim: The earlier an individual with a congenital limb difference was fitted with an artificial arm, the better their motor control was.
source: However, the earlier an individual with a congenital limb difference was fitted with an artificial arm, the better their motor control was.
evidence: Based on correlation analysis between age at first artificial arm use and reaching errors

claim: No group differences were found when reaching without visual feedback.
source: Since we found no group differences when reaching without visual feedback, we suggest that the ability to perform efficient visual-based corrective movements is highly dependent on either biological or artificial arm experience at a very young age.
evidence: Based on experimental data from the 2D localization task

claim: The ability to perform efficient visual-based corrective movements is highly dependent on either biological or artificial arm experience at a very young age.
source: Since we found no group differences when reaching without visual feedback, we suggest that the ability to perform efficient visual-based corrective movements is highly dependent on either biological or artificial arm experience at a very young age.
evidence: Inferred from the pattern of results showing deficits with visual feedback but not without

claim: Opportunities for sensorimotor plasticity become more limited with age.
source: Subsequently, opportunities for sensorimotor plasticity become more limited.
evidence: Inferred from the relationship between age at first artificial arm use and motor control

claim: All included participants were able to control the robotic handle and perform the task using the same speed-accuracy trade-off parameters following Fitts' Law.
source: All included participants were able to control the robotic handle and perform the task using the same speed-accuracy trade-off parameters following Fitts' Law (see Appendix 1).
evidence: Based on analysis of participant performance data

claim: There was no significant group effect when comparing the absolute errors of the intact arm and dominant arm across the three groups.
source: We found no significant group effect (F(2,48)=1.05, p=−0.14) when comparing the absolute errors of the intact arm and dominant arm across the three groups (control, acquired, and congenital groups).
evidence: Based on statistical analysis of intact arm performance data

claim: The result regarding intact arm performance was inconclusive (neither supporting null nor alternative hypothesis).
source: However, this result was inconclusive (BF10=0.65), that is, supports neither the null nor the alternative hypothesis.
evidence: Based on Bayesian statistical analysis

claim: There was a significant effect of intact-hand performance on artificial arm errors.
source: We found a significant effect of intact-hand performance (F(1,47)=28.65, p<0.001, ηp2=0.38), that is, participants who had small errors with their intact arm also tended to have smaller errors with their nondominant/artificial arm.
evidence: Based on ANCOVA statistical analysis

claim: Participants who had small errors with their intact arm also tended to have smaller errors with their nondominant/artificial arm.
source: We found a significant effect of intact-hand performance (F(1,47)=28.65, p<0.001, ηp2=0.38), that is, participants who had small errors with their intact arm also tended to have smaller errors with their nondominant/artificial arm.
evidence: Based on ANCOVA statistical analysis showing correlation between intact and artificial arm performance

claim: There was a significant group effect for artificial arm reaching performance (F(2,47)=13.81, p<0.001, ηp2=0.37).
source: We found a significant group effect (F(2,47)=13.81, p<0.001, ηp2=0.37), indicating the groups differed in their visuomotor performance with their artificial arm (or nondominant arm in controls).
evidence: Based on ANCOVA statistical analysis

claim: The congenital group exhibited larger errors with their artificial arm compared to the artificial arm of the acquired group (t=−3.77, ptukey=0.001, Cohen's-d=−1.39).
source: Post hoc comparisons revealed that the congenital group exhibited larger errors with their artificial arm compared to both the artificial arm of the acquired group (t=−3.77, ptukey=0.001, Cohen's-d=−1.39), and the nondominant arm of the control group (t=−5.06, ptukey<0.001, Cohen's-d=−1.705).
evidence: Based on post hoc statistical comparisons

claim: The congenital group exhibited larger errors with their artificial arm compared to the nondominant arm of the control group (t=−5.06, ptukey<0.001, Cohen's-d=−1.705).
source: Post hoc comparisons revealed that the congenital group exhibited larger errors with their artificial arm compared to both the artificial arm of the acquired group (t=−3.77, ptukey=0.001, Cohen's-d=−1.39), and the nondominant arm of the control group (t=−5.06, ptukey<0.001, Cohen's-d=−1.705).
evidence: Based on post hoc statistical comparisons

claim: The acquired group's artificial arm errors did not differ from those of the control group's nondominant arm (t=−0.885, ptukey=0.65).
source: Conversely, the acquired group's artificial arm errors did not differ from those of the control group's nondominant arm (t=−0.885, ptukey=0.65), indicating a specific deficit in error reaching for the congenital groups' artificial arm.
evidence: Based on post hoc statistical comparisons

claim: Bayesian analysis provided moderate support to the null hypothesis that the acquired and control groups perform similarly (BF10=0.28).
source: The resulting Bayesian Factor (BF10=0.28) provided moderate support to the null hypothesis (i.e., smaller than 0.33).
evidence: Based on Bayesian statistical analysis

claim: The congenital group shows significantly inferior artificial arm reaching accuracy compared to the other groups.
source: To summarize, the congenital group shows significantly inferior artificial arm reaching accuracy in our task compared to the other groups (see Supplementary file 1a for results of the statistical analyses confirming that this effect was not driven by the side (L/R) of the artificial arm/nondominant side).
evidence: Based on statistical analyses of reaching performance data

claim: Across both acquired and congenital groups, the correlation between absolute reaching error and residual limb length was not significant (rs(30)=−0.23, p=0.2).
source: Across both acquired and congenital groups, the correlation between absolute reaching error and either residual limb length was not significant (rs(30)=−0.23, p=0.2).
evidence: Based on correlation analysis

claim: Residual limb length does not play a significant role in the observed group effect for endpoint accuracy of artificial arm reaches.
source: Therefore, the length of the residual limb does not play a significant role in the observed group effect for endpoint accuracy of artificial arm reaches.
evidence: Based on ANCOVA analysis including residual limb length as covariate

claim: The type of device used does not influence endpoint reaching error in the task (F(2,29)=0.435, p=0.65, BF10=0.275).
source: Despite the differences in appearance and control mechanisms between devices, the type of device used does not seem to influence endpoint reaching error in our task, as demonstrated by a one-way ANOVA with device type as a between-subject variable showing no significant differences between devices (F(2,29)=0.435, p=0.65, BF10=0.275).
evidence: Based on one-way ANOVA statistical analysis

claim: No significant differences in bias angle were found between the groups (Watson-Williams circular test: F(2,48)=1.95, p=0.15).
source: We found no significant differences in bias angle between the groups (Watson-Williams circular test: F(2,48)=1.95, p=0.15).
evidence: Based on Watson-Williams circular test analysis, shown in Figure 2A

claim: No significant group differences were found for bias (F(2,47)=2.40, p=0.1, BFIncl=0.72).
source: We compared artificial arm and nondominant arm biases (distance from the center of the endpoint to the target) across groups, using intact arm biases as a covariate. The ANCOVA resulted in no significant (inconclusive) group differences (F(2,47)=2.40, p=0.1, BFIncl=0.72; see Figure 2A).
evidence: Based on ANCOVA statistical analysis, shown in Figure 2A

claim: A significant group effect was found for motor noise (F(2,47)=13.205, p<0.001, ηp2=0.36).
source: When comparing artificial arm and nondominant arm motor noise (spatial standard deviation [SD] of endpoints relative to the center of the endpoints), using intact-hand noise as a covariate, we found a significant group effect (F(2,47)=13.205, p<0.001, ηp2=0.36; see Figure 2A).
evidence: Based on ANCOVA statistical analysis, shown in Figure 2A

claim: The congenital group exhibited larger motor noise with their artificial arm compared to the artificial arm of the acquired group (t=−2.90, ptukey=0.015, Cohen's-d=−0.855).
source: Reflecting the absolute error findings, the congenital group exhibited larger motor noise with their artificial arm compared to the artificial arm of the acquired group (t=−2.90, ptukey=0.015, Cohen's-d=−0.855), and the nondominant arm of control group (t=−5.31, ptukey<0.001, Cohen's-d=−1.65).
evidence: Based on post hoc statistical comparisons

claim: The congenital group exhibited larger motor noise with their artificial arm compared to the nondominant arm of control group (t=−5.31, ptukey<0.001, Cohen's-d=−1.65).
source: Reflecting the absolute error findings, the congenital group exhibited larger motor noise with their artificial arm compared to the artificial arm of the acquired group (t=−2.90, ptukey=0.015, Cohen's-d=−0.855), and the nondominant arm of control group (t=−5.31, ptukey<0.001, Cohen's-d=−1.65).
evidence: Based on post hoc statistical comparisons

claim: Comparing motor noise between amputees' artificial arm and controls' nondominant arm was inconclusive (t=−2.1, ptukey=0.1, BF10=1.2).
source: Comparing motor noise between amputees' artificial arm and controls' nondominant arm was inconclusive (t=−2.1, ptukey=0.1, BF10=1.2).
evidence: Based on statistical comparison and Bayesian analysis

claim: The congenital group's artificial arm reaches are best characterized by increased noise (endpoint variability).
source: These results show that the congenital group's artificial arm reaches are best characterized by increased noise (endpoint variability).
evidence: Inferred from the pattern of statistical results showing significant noise differences but not bias differences

claim: Commercially available artificial arms currently lack direct sensory feedback.
source: Commercially available artificial arms, as the ones used by our participants, currently lack direct sensory feedback, and of most relevance to reaching, proprioceptive feedback.
evidence: Based on established knowledge about current artificial arm technology

claim: Proprioception provides an essential input to the sensorimotor system.
source: Proprioception, the sense of position and movement of our body, provides an essential input to the sensorimotor system (Sarlegna and Sainburg, 2009; Wolpert et al., 1995).
evidence: Supported by citations to Sarlegna and Sainburg, 2009; Wolpert et al., 1995

claim: Proprioception together with vision is used to accurately localize the current position of the arm and guides corrective movement during the execution of reaching movements.
source: Together with vision, it is used to accurately localize the current position of the arm and guides corrective movement during the execution of reaching movements.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of sensorimotor control

claim: No localization differences were found between the congenital and acquired groups for residual limb localization (Mann-Whitney W=112.5, p=0.46, BF10=0.26).
source: Interestingly, we found no localization differences between the congenital and acquired groups in either condition (Residual limb: Mann-Whitney W=112.5, p=0.46, BF10=0.26; Artificial arm: Mann-Whitney W=104.5, p=0.7, BF10=0.24; see Figure 2C), suggesting that individuals with a congenital limb difference are equally able as individuals with an acquired limb difference at localizing their artificial arm.
evidence: Based on Mann-Whitney statistical test, shown in Figure 2C

claim: No localization differences were found between the congenital and acquired groups for artificial arm localization (Mann-Whitney W=104.5, p=0.7, BF10=0.24).
source: Interestingly, we found no localization differences between the congenital and acquired groups in either condition (Residual limb: Mann-Whitney W=112.5, p=0.46, BF10=0.26; Artificial arm: Mann-Whitney W=104.5, p=0.7, BF10=0.24; see Figure 2C), suggesting that individuals with a congenital limb difference are equally able as individuals with an acquired limb difference at localizing their artificial arm.
evidence: Based on Mann-Whitney statistical test, shown in Figure 2C

claim: Individuals with a congenital limb difference are equally able as individuals with an acquired limb difference at localizing their artificial arm.
source: Interestingly, we found no localization differences between the congenital and acquired groups in either condition (Residual limb: Mann-Whitney W=112.5, p=0.46, BF10=0.26; Artificial arm: Mann-Whitney W=104.5, p=0.7, BF10=0.24; see Figure 2C), suggesting that individuals with a congenital limb difference are equally able as individuals with an acquired limb difference at localizing their artificial arm.
evidence: Inferred from the lack of significant differences in localization tasks

claim: Participants made larger errors in the 2D localization task compared to the main task.
source: Overall, participants made larger errors and took longer to get to the target (movement time) in this task compared to the main task (see Supplementary file 1d&e for full statistical analysis showing a significant task effect for both measures).
evidence: Based on statistical comparison between tasks

claim: Participants took longer to get to the target in the 2D localization task compared to the main task.
source: Overall, participants made larger errors and took longer to get to the target (movement time) in this task compared to the main task (see Supplementary file 1d&e for full statistical analysis showing a significant task effect for both measures).
evidence: Based on statistical comparison between tasks

claim: No group differences were found in artificial arm errors in the 2D localization task (F(2,44)=0.71, p=0.5, BFIncl=0.33).
source: Using the same ANCOVA approach described above, we compared artificial arm (and nondominant arm) errors of the three groups, while controlling for intact-hand performance as a covariate. We found no group differences in artificial arm errors (F(2,44)=0.71, p=0.5, BFIncl=0.33; see Figure 2D).
evidence: Based on ANCOVA statistical analysis, shown in Figure 2D

claim: There was no significant difference between the artificial arm performance of the congenital and acquired groups in the 2D localization task (t 0.71, punc=0.48, BF10=0.25).
source: We further performed a planned pairwise comparison between the artificial arm performance of the congenital and acquired groups and found no significant difference (t 0.71, punc=0.48, BF10=0.25).
evidence: Based on pairwise statistical comparison

claim: The congenital group's artificial arm localization is not substantially different than that of amputees.
source: Taken together, these results suggest that the congenital group's artificial arm localization is not substantially different than that of amputees.
evidence: Inferred from the lack of significant differences in localization tasks

claim: Fast reaching movements can be roughly divided into an initial impulse phase and an error correction phase.
source: Fast reaching movements, such as the ones performed in our main task, can be roughly divided into two phases: an initial impulse phase that involves the execution of a motor plan constructed prior to movement initiation and an error correction phase where sensory information is used to correct errors during execution (Elliott et al., 2001).
evidence: Supported by citation to Elliott et al., 2001

claim: The timing of peak velocity in reaching movements is often used as a time point that mostly reflects the feedforward phase.
source: The timing of peak velocity in such a movement is often used as a time point that mostly reflects the first phase, that is, the trajectory up to this point is mostly governed by feedforward mechanisms (Krakauer et al., 1999; Patterson et al., 2017; Sainburg et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by citations to Krakauer et al., 1999; Patterson et al., 2017; Sainburg et al., 2003

claim: Significant group differences were found in artificial arm initial directional errors (F(2,47)=8.01, p<0.001, ηp2=0.26).
source: As with previous measures, initial directional errors were analyzed using an ANCOVA comparing directional errors of the artificial arm (and nondominant arm) of the three groups, while controlling for intact-hand directional errors as a covariate. We found significant group differences in artificial arm errors (F(2,47)=8.01, p<0.001, ηp2=0.26).
evidence: Based on ANCOVA statistical analysis

claim: The congenital group exhibited larger directional errors with their artificial arm compared to the acquired group (t=−3.515, p=0.003, Cohen's-d=−1.10).
source: The congenital group exhibited larger directional errors with their artificial arm compared to the acquired group (t=−3.515, p=0.003, Cohen's-d=−1.10) and the control group (t=−3.31, p=0.005, Cohen's-d=−0.98).
evidence: Based on post hoc statistical comparisons

claim: The congenital group exhibited larger directional errors with their artificial arm compared to the control group (t=−3.31, p=0.005, Cohen's-d=−0.98).

evidence: Based on post hoc statistical comparisons

claim: The acquired group's artificial arm directional errors did not differ from those of the nondominant arm of the control group (t=0.16, p=0.9, BF10=0.21).
source: The acquired group's artificial arm directional errors did not differ from those of the nondominant arm of the control group (t=0.16, p=0.9, BF10=0.21).

source: This result suggests that the initial motor plan of the congenital group differs from that of the acquired and control groups.
evidence: Inferred from the significant differences in initial directional errors

claim: Inconclusive evidence was found for group differences in artificial arm corrective angles (F(2,47)=2.19, p=0.12, BFIncl=0.67).
source: Using the same ANCOVA approach described above, we found inconclusive evidence for group differences in artificial arm corrective angles (F(2,47)=2.19, p=0.12, BFIncl=0.67).
evidence: Based on ANCOVA statistical analysis

claim: Within the congenital group, corrective angles were highly correlated with initial error angle (r(16)=0.76, p<0.001).
source: Within the congenital group, corrective angles were highly correlated with initial error angle (r(16)=0.76, p<0.001) and not correlated with motor variability (r(16)=0.35, p=0.16, BF10=0.73).
evidence: Based on correlation analysis

claim: Within the congenital group, corrective angles were not correlated with motor variability (r(16)=0.35, p=0.16, BF10=0.73).
source: Within the congenital group, corrective angles were highly correlated with initial error angle (r(16)=0.76, p<0.001) and not correlated with motor variability (r(16)=0.35, p=0.16, BF10=0.73).

claim: Individuals who made larger initial errors had more to correct for and therefore showed bigger corrective movements.
source: In other words, individuals who made larger initial errors had more to correct for and therefore showed bigger corrective movements.
evidence: Inferred from the correlation between initial error and corrective angle

claim: Individuals who made larger corrective movements were not necessarily more accurate in reaching the target.
source: However, individuals who made larger corrective movements were not necessarily more accurate in reaching the target.
evidence: Inferred from the lack of correlation between corrective movements and motor variability

claim: The congenital group has accumulated on average approximately 29 more years of artificial arm experience compared to the acquired group (t(30)=−7.86, p<0.001).
source: First, we confirmed that although the congenital group has accumulated on average ~29 more years of (intermittent) artificial arm experience compared to the acquired group (t(30)=−7.86, p<0.001), there are no differences in artificial arm daily usage between the two artificial arm users' groups, as assessed using questionnaires (acquired vs. congenital groups; t(30)=−0.25, p=0.81, BF10=0.35).

claim: There are no differences in artificial arm daily usage between the acquired and congenital groups (t(30)=−0.25, p=0.81, BF10=0.35).

claim: No relationship was found between artificial arm reaching errors and daily life artificial arm usage score (r(30)=−0.05, p=0.78, BF10=0.23).

claim: A relationship was found between daily life artificial arm usage and intact-hand reaching errors across acquired and congenital groups (r(39)=−0.41, p=0.008).

claim: Smaller intact-hand errors (higher accuracy) were associated with higher artificial arm use scores (more versatile and frequent use).
source: Smaller intact-hand errors (higher accuracy) were associated with higher artificial arm use scores (more versatile and frequent use).

claim: There is a relationship between an individual's general motor control (as measured by their intact arm) and their ability to use an artificial arm.
source: While being cautious not to infer causality from a correlation, we believe this result uncovers a relationship between an individual's general motor control (as measured by their intact arm) and their ability to use an artificial arm.

claim: A significant positive correlation was found between age at first artificial arm use and artificial arm reaching errors in the congenital group (rs(16)=0.57, p=0.01).
source: Interestingly, we found a significant positive correlation between age at first artificial arm use and artificial arm reaching errors (rs(16)=0.57, p=0.01; see Figure 1D).

claim: Individuals who started using an artificial arm at an earlier age produced smaller errors with their current artificial arm as adults.
source: Individuals who started using an artificial arm at an earlier age produced smaller errors with their current artificial arm as adults.

claim: Our ability to adjust our motor representation might not be as flexible as we thought and might be constrained by early life experience.
source: This result suggests that our ability to adjust our motor representation might not be as flexible as we thought and might be constrained by early life experience.

source: Finally, we did not find a significant relationship between past (age at first artificial arm use) and present (daily life use score) artificial arm experience (rs(16)=−0.03, p=0.91) or between artificial arm reaching errors and elapsed time since first artificial arm use (r(16)=0.01, p=0.96, BF10=0.29).

claim: No significant relationship was found between artificial arm reaching errors and elapsed time since first artificial arm use (r(16)=0.01, p=0.96, BF10=0.29).

claim: Individuals who started using an artificial arm earlier in life showed less endpoint motor noise in the reaching task.
source: That is, individuals who started using an artificial arm earlier in life also showed less endpoint motor noise in the reaching task.
evidence: Based on correlation analysis between age at first use and motor noise

claim: Initial directional error did not significantly correlate with age at first artificial arm use in the congenital group (rs(16)=0.38, pbonf=0.74).
source: While we did find group differences in initial directional errors (as reported in The congenital group shows larger artificial arm initial directional errors), it did not significantly correlate with age at first artificial arm use (rs(16)=0.38, pbonf=0.74).
evidence: Based on correlation analysis

claim: Early life experience relates to a suboptimal ability to reduce the system's inherent noise.
source: From these results, we infer that early life experience relates to a suboptimal ability to reduce the system's inherent noise, and that this is possibly not related to the noise generated by the execution of the initial motor plan.
evidence: Inferred from the correlation between age at first use and motor noise but not initial directional error

claim: Early life experience might relate to better use of visual feedback in performing corrective movements.
source: Early life experience might therefore relate to better use of visual feedback in performing corrective movements.
evidence: Inferred from the pattern of results showing noise relates to early experience

claim: Limited early life experience results in suboptimal integration of visual and sensory information within the sensorimotor system.
source: Therefore, one possibility is that limited early life experience, results in suboptimal integration of visual and sensory information within the sensorimotor system.
evidence: Speculative interpretation of the results

claim: No correlation was found between artificial arm errors and age at first artificial arm use in the acquired group (rs(12)=−0.23, p=0.43).
source: However, we found no such correlation between artificial arm errors and age at first artificial arm use in the acquired group (rs(12)=−0.23, p=0.43).
evidence: Based on correlation analysis

claim: A significant positive correlation was found between artificial arm absolute errors and years of limbless experience in the acquired group (rs(12)=0.71, p=0.005).
source: Here, we find a significant positive correlation between artificial arm absolute errors and years of limbless experience (rs(12)=0.71, p=0.005; see Figure 3).
evidence: Based on correlation analysis, shown in Figure 3

claim: The sooner an individual with an acquired limb difference was fitted with an artificial arm after amputation, the smaller errors they made with their current artificial arm years later.
source: The sooner an individual with an acquired limb difference was fitted with an artificial arm after amputation, the smaller errors they made with their current artificial arm years later.
evidence: Based on correlation analysis between years of limbless experience and errors

claim: In the acquired group, motor noise was significantly correlated with years of limbless experience (rs(12)=0.85, pbonf=0.03).
source: Similar to the congenital group, this relationship appears to be driven by motor noise and not by bias. Motor noise was significantly correlated with years of limbless experience (rs(12)=0.85, pbonf=0.03; see Figure 3), while bias did not (rs(12)=0.32, pbonf=1; comparing between correlations: Z=2.9, p=0.003).
evidence: Based on correlation analysis, shown in Figure 3

claim: In the acquired group, bias was not significantly correlated with years of limbless experience (rs(12)=0.32, pbonf=1).
source: Similar to the congenital group, this relationship appears to be driven by motor noise and not by bias. Motor noise was significantly correlated with years of limbless experience (rs(12)=0.85, pbonf=0.03; see Figure 3), while bias did not (rs(12)=0.32, pbonf=1; comparing between correlations: Z=2.9, p=0.003).
evidence: Based on correlation analysis

claim: The amount of time an individual spends using their residual limb before starting to use an artificial arm has a long-lasting effect on their ability to control an artificial arm in terms of motor noise.
source: Although the type of plasticity bottlenecks in each group might be different, it appears that the amount of time an individual spends using their residual limb before starting to use an artificial arm has a long-lasting effect, in terms of motor noise, on their ability to control an artificial arm.
evidence: Inferred from the correlations found in both groups between time before first use and motor noise

claim: Infants' reaches are surprisingly functional.
source: While infants' reaches are surprisingly functional (Babinsky et al., 2012; von Hofsten, 1980), they take a considerable amount of time to be fine-tuned.
evidence: Supported by citations to Babinsky et al., 2012; von Hofsten, 1980

claim: There are multiple, non-linear developmental processes occurring until at least the age of approximately 12 years.
source: There are multiple, non-linear (Olivier et al., 2007) developmental processes occurring until at least the age of ~12 years (Schneiberg et al., 2002; Simon-Martinez et al., 2018; Sveistrup et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to developmental studies

claim: The congenital group performed worse than the acquired group in the visuomotor precision reaching task.
source: In this context, it may not be surprising that we found that individuals with a congenital limb difference, who started using an artificial arm in early childhood, performed differently in a visuomotor precision reaching task, relative to individuals with an acquired limb difference, who only began to use an artificial arm in adulthood (age range=19–56, mean=32). Yet, contrary to our expectation, the congenital group performed worse than the acquired group, who in turn did not show any deficits in controlling their artificial arm relative to two-handed controls using their nondominant arm.
evidence: Based on experimental results from the main task

claim: The acquired group did not show any deficits in controlling their artificial arm relative to two-handed controls using their nondominant arm.
source: Yet, contrary to our expectation, the congenital group performed worse than the acquired group, who in turn did not show any deficits in controlling their artificial arm relative to two-handed controls using their nondominant arm.
evidence: Based on experimental results from the main task

claim: Increased experience with an artificial arm did not lead to better performance.
source: The observed difference between the two artificial arm user's groups, and the fact that increased experience with an artificial arm did not lead to better performance, is also in stark contrast with the notion that our internal model flexibly scales with the endpoint of the tool, as we use it (Miller et al., 2018).
evidence: Based on the lack of correlation between usage and performance

claim: The congenital group's initial directional error is greater than that of the acquired group.
source: Our analysis points at potential deficits in this internal model, as the congenital group's initial directional error—reflecting the execution of an initial motor plan and thought to precede sensory feedback—is greater than that of the acquired group.
evidence: Based on statistical analysis of initial directional errors

claim: Individuals with a congenital limb difference may not be able to refine their model enough to create an accurate template of their artificial arm.
source: If true, this suggests that individuals with a congenital limb difference may not be able to refine their model enough to create an accurate template of their artificial arm.
evidence: Speculative interpretation of the initial directional error results

claim: When performing reaching movements without visual feedback, the congenital group did not differ from the acquired or control group.
source: When performing reaching movements without visual feedback (2D localization task), the congenital group did not differ from the acquired or control group.
evidence: Based on statistical analysis of the 2D localization task

claim: The proprioceptive and somatosensory feedback from the residual limb appears to be enough to allow the congenital group to correct for initial reaching errors and perform at the same level as the acquired and control groups in the 2D localization task.
source: While they did not receive visual feedback, the proprioceptive and somatosensory feedback from the residual limb appears to be enough to allow them to correct for initial reaching errors and perform at the same level as the acquired and control groups.
evidence: Inferred from the lack of group differences in the 2D localization task

claim: The process of using visual information to perform corrective movements is not as efficient in the congenital group.
source: As such, by elimination, our evidence suggests that the process of using visual information to perform corrective movements is not as efficient in the congenital group.
evidence: Inferred from the pattern of results across different tasks

claim: Individuals with a congenital limb difference have impaired processing of visual hand information.
source: This idea is consistent with previous evidence showing individuals with a congenital limb difference have impaired processing of visual hand information (Maimon-Mor et al., 2020b).
evidence: Supported by citation to Maimon-Mor et al., 2020b

claim: A brief period of postnatal visual deprivation caused long-lasting (though mild) alterations to visuo-auditory processing.
source: This interpretation is also compatible with previous studies in individuals experiencing a brief period of postnatal visual deprivation which caused long-lasting (though mild) alterations to visuo-auditory processing (de Heering et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to de Heering et al., 2016

claim: The ability to optimally integrate visual information continues to develop way into childhood.
source: While the maturation of the vision system occurs much earlier than that of motor control, the ability to optimally integrate visual information continues to develop way into childhood (Contreras-Vidal, 2006; Contreras-Vidal et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations to Contreras-Vidal, 2006; Contreras-Vidal et al., 2005

claim: Lack of concurrent visual and motor experience during development might cause a deficit in the ability to form the computational substrates to efficiently use visual information in performing corrective movements.
source: Lack of concurrent visual and motor experience during development might therefore cause a deficit in the ability to form the computational substrates and thus to efficiently use visual information in performing corrective movements.
evidence: Speculative interpretation based on developmental literature and study results

claim: Endpoint noise, and not initial directional error, associates with age at first artificial arm use.
source: Indeed, we found that endpoint noise, and not initial directional error, associates with age at first artificial arm use.
evidence: Based on correlation analyses

claim: One's ability to efficiently integrate sensory information with motor control might relate to early life experience with an artificial arm.
source: This, too, supports the idea that one's ability to efficiently integrate sensory information with motor control might relate to early life experience with an artificial arm.
evidence: Inferred from the correlation between age at first use and motor noise

claim: Early life experience with an artificial arm was not a good indicator for successful current artificial arm adoption in the dataset.
source: In our data set, early life experience with an artificial arm was not a good indicator for successful current artificial arm adoption, however our limited sample size and inclusion criteria of only including individuals who currently use an artificial arm prevents us for making direct clinical recommendations.
evidence: Based on the lack of correlation between age at first use and current usage

claim: The relationship between intact-arm performance and current artificial arm use in both the acquired and congenital groups is of interest to artificial arm rehabilitation.
source: The relationship between intact-arm performance and current artificial arm use in both the acquired and congenital groups is also of interest to artificial arm rehabilitation and should be taken into account in future studies.
evidence: Based on the correlation found between intact-arm performance and usage

claim: The formation of an arm representation in early life has a long-lasting effect on the incorporation of an artificial arm.
source: Our results suggest that the formation of an arm representation in early life has a long-lasting effect on the incorporation of an artificial arm, highlighting that opportunities for sensorimotor plasticity become more limited with age, even across early childhood.
evidence: Inferred from the overall pattern of results showing effects of early experience

claim: Opportunities for sensorimotor plasticity become more limited with age, even across early childhood.
source: Our results suggest that the formation of an arm representation in early life has a long-lasting effect on the incorporation of an artificial arm, highlighting that opportunities for sensorimotor plasticity become more limited with age, even across early childhood.
evidence: Inferred from the correlation between age at first use and motor control

claim: Forty-four artificial arm users were recruited for this study.
source: Forty-four artificial arm users were recruited for this study: 21 individuals with a unilateral acquired limb difference following amputation (mean age±std=48.67±12.9, 18 males, 12 with intact right arm), and 23 individuals with a congenital unilateral upper-limb limb difference (transverse deficiency; age±std=46.09±11.22, 11 males, 17 with intact right arm; see Table 1 for full demographic details).
evidence: Based on study recruitment

claim: Seven participants were excluded from all analyses.
source: Seven participants were excluded from all analyses: four participants with a trans-humeral limb loss (three amputees) were not able to perform the tasks with their artificial arm. Two participants (one amputee) had trouble controlling the robotic handle with their artificial arm and therefore their artificial arm reaches data in both tasks has been excluded. Data from all tasks involving the robotic manipulandum of one participant (congenital group) was excluded, due to technical issues with the robotic device.
evidence: Based on data quality control procedures

claim: Twenty age, gender, and handedness matched two-handed controls were recruited for this study.
source: Additionally, 20 age, gender, and handedness matched two-handed controls were recruited for this study (mean age±std=42.55±15.5, 11 males, 14 with a dominant right arm).
evidence: Based on study recruitment

claim: Participants were recruited to the study between October 2017 and December 2018.
source: Participants were recruited to the study between October 2017 and December 2018, based on the guidelines in our ethical approvals (UCL REC: 9937/001; NHS National Research Ethics service: 18/LO/0474), and in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki.
evidence: Based on study documentation

claim: A maximum movement time of 1 s per reach was imposed to encourage participants to perform fast-reaching movements.
source: To encourage participants to perform fast-reaching movements, a maximum movement time of 1 s per reach was imposed.
evidence: Based on experimental design

claim: Movement initiation was defined by arm velocity exceeding 3.5 cm/s starting from the time of participants' first movement, following the presentation of the target.
source: Movement initiation was defined by arm velocity exceeding 3.5 cm/s starting from the time of participants' first movement, following the presentation of the target.
evidence: Based on data processing methodology

claim: Velocity data were smoothed using an 8 Hz low-pass Butterworth filter.
source: Velocity data were smoothed using an 8 Hz low-pass Butterworth filter (Przybyla et al., 2013).
evidence: Based on data processing methodology, with citation to Przybyla et al., 2013

claim: Movement termination was defined by the first minimum with a velocity smaller than 50% of the peak velocity.
source: Movement termination was defined by the first minimum with a velocity smaller than 50% of the peak velocity.
evidence: Based on data processing methodology

claim: An average of 1.1 and 1.4 trials per participant were excluded for the intact and artificial arm, respectively, with a range of 0–7.
source: An average of 1.1 and 1.4 trials per participant were excluded for the intact and artificial arm, respectively, with a range of 0–7.
evidence: Based on data quality control

claim: There were no group differences in the amount of excluded trials.
source: There were no group differences in the amount of excluded trials.
evidence: Based on statistical comparison

claim: Two participants from the acquired group and two participants from the congenital group did not take part in the 1D localization task as it was introduced later in the data collection process.
source: Two participants from the acquired group and two participants from the congenital group did not take part in this task as it was introduced later in the data collection process.
evidence: Based on study procedures

claim: In the 2D localization task, each of the 60 targets used in the main task was repeated twice (i.e., a total of 120 trials for each arm).
source: Due to the noisier nature of these reaches, each of the 60 targets used in the main task was repeated twice (i.e., a total of 120 trials for each arm).
evidence: Based on experimental design

claim: An average of 1.35 and 1.5 trials per participant were excluded for the intact and artificial arm in the 2D localization task, respectively, with a range of 0–13.
source: An average of 1.35 and 1.5 trials per participant were excluded for the intact and artificial arm, respectively, with a range of 0–13.
evidence: Based on data quality control

claim: Artificial arm scores were calculated for the most used artificial arm.
source: Artificial arm scores were calculated for the most used artificial arm, wear time and PAL were standardized using a Z-transform and summed to create an artificial arm usage score that reflects the frequency of use and incorporation of the artificial arm in activities of daily living.
evidence: Based on data analysis methodology

claim: The artificial arm usage measures have been previously shown to have good reliability using a test-retest assessment.
source: These measures have been previously shown to have good reliability using a test-retest assessment (Maimon-Mor et al., 2020c).
evidence: Supported by citation to Maimon-Mor et al., 2020c

claim: Absolute error measures were logarithmically transformed and then averaged in order to correct for the skewed error distribution and satisfy the conditions for parametric statistical testing.
source: Absolute error measures were logarithmically transformed and then averaged in order to correct for the skewed error distribution and satisfy the conditions for parametric statistical testing.
evidence: Based on statistical analysis methodology

claim: In the main task, two participants (one from the acquired group, one from the congenital group) were excluded due to their high artificial arm errors.
source: Following this outlier criteria, in the main task, two participants (one from the acquired group, one from the congenital group) were excluded due to their high artificial arm errors.
evidence: Based on data quality control procedures

claim: For the 2D localization task, three participants (two from the acquired group, one from the control group) were excluded due to their high intact-arm errors.
source: For the 2D localization task, three participants (two from the acquired group, one from the control group) were excluded due to their high intact-arm errors.
evidence: Based on data quality control procedures

claim: A BF<0.33 is interpreted as support for the null hypothesis.
source: A BF<0.33 is interpreted as support for the null hypothesis, BF>3 is interpreted as support for the alternative hypothesis (Dienes, 2014).
evidence: Based on established Bayesian statistical interpretation guidelines, with citation to Dienes, 2014

claim: A BF>3 is interpreted as support for the alternative hypothesis.
source: A BF<0.33 is interpreted as support for the null hypothesis, BF>3 is interpreted as support for the alternative hypothesis (Dienes, 2014).
evidence: Based on established Bayesian statistical interpretation guidelines, with citation to Dienes, 2014
